title: Fitting anti-peck devices to hens
subtitle: Using blinders and beak bits to interrupt feather-pecking without beak trimming.
excerpt: Anti-peck devices are small plastic clips or rings that fit over the beak or nostrils and interrupt a hen's forward vision just enough to prevent accurate pecking at another bird. They are a last resort for persistent feather-pecking that has not responded to management changes, and they work best when fitted early, before an established pecking habit takes hold.
sourceNotes: RSPCA Assured chicken welfare standards (2023). DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Laying Hens (2018). Compassion in World Farming, feather pecking management guide (2022). University of Bristol Veterinary School, feather pecking research summary (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: A behavioural problem in poultry where birds peck at and pull feathers from other birds. It can become a welfare emergency when it progresses to skin damage and blood, which attracts further pecking.

A small plastic device that clips through the nostrils and extends over the tip of the upper beak, disrupting the angle of the beak just enough to prevent accurate feather-pecking while allowing normal feeding and drinking.

content.text: Anti-peck devices sit between management changes and culling in a
feather-pecking
flock. Address the cause first: overcrowding, perch space, nutrition, light. If pecking has become a habit, a
bumpa-bit
or blinder can break the cycle. It avoids the need for beak trimming.
Types of device

Bumpa-bits: plastic clips that pass through a small hole in the bird's upper nostril septum. They tip the beak angle slightly forward, making accurate forward-directed pecking difficult. Birds can still eat and drink normally from ground-level feeders.

Blinders (spectacles): plastic wings that clip to the beak and partially obstruct forward vision without blocking it entirely. The bird can still see to move and eat but cannot focus directly forward to peck.

Pinless peepers: plastic clips that fit over the nostrils with wing-like blinkers on each side, similar to blinkers on a horse. They obstruct side-forward vision on a bird that habitually turns its head to peck.
Before fitting

Identify which bird or birds are the primary peckers, not the victims. In most flocks, one or two initiators drive the pecking. Fitting all birds is rarely necessary. Isolate the victim with one or two calm birds for a few days while wounds heal; then reintroduce once the pecker is fitted.
Fitting a bumpa-bit
Catch the bird and hold her firmly between your knees, facing away from you, wings held against her body.

Push the pin of the bumpa-bit through the small hole at the base of the upper beak (the soft septum between the nostrils). Use the supplied applicator tool rather than a pin: a clean through-pass causes less tissue trauma.
Clip the locking piece over the pin on the other side of the septum. It should sit flat against the nasal tissue without pulling tight.
Release the bird and watch her eat and drink immediately. She will shake her head a few times and then adapt. Check that water drinkers have sufficient depth for her to drink with the bit in place.

Anti-peck devices are not a permanent solution in a poorly managed flock. Once the habit is broken after two to four weeks, remove the device and reassess the environment. If feather-pecking restarts within days, the underlying cause has not been addressed.
Care after fitting
Check fitted birds daily for the first week. Look for any sign of nostril tissue infection, difficulty eating, or withdrawal from the flock.
Ensure feeder and drinker design suits fitted birds. Nipple drinkers are difficult to use with a bumpa-bit; a shallow open drinker or bell drinker is better.
Remove the device after three to four weeks. If feather-pecking recurs, the management environment needs further attention, not a permanent fit.

attrs.cue: Bird is not eating after fitting
attrs.cause: Bit is too tight, impeding beak movement; or bird cannot reach the feeder type with the bit in place
attrs.fix: Check the bit for excessive tightness: there should be a slight gap between the bit and the nostril tissue. Switch to a ground-level feeder so the bird can eat without angling her head.

attrs.cue: Feather-pecking continues despite fitted bird wearing the device
attrs.cause: The fitted bird is not the primary pecker, or there is more than one initiator in the flock
attrs.fix: Observe the flock for an hour. Identify who is initiating pecking now. A blinder or bumpa-bit does not stop a determined pecker who can still manoeuvre to attack from the side.
